# How to Practice a Salary Negotiation Out Loud with an AI Coach

> **In short:** You can rehearse a salary chat with any AI assistant — open a fresh conversation, set up a role-play, then speak or type through the awkward moments. It won't promise you'll get the raise, but you'll sound clearer and calmer in the real talk.

Most salary talks don't fall apart because of the number. They fall apart because nobody has said the words out loud before the meeting. Your voice shakes, you apologize, you take the first "no" as the final answer. That's fixable. With any AI assistant that has chat or voice — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat, DeepSeek or similar — you can run through the whole conversation in private first: the opening line, the pushback, the moment they say "we don't have budget". By the time you sit down with your manager, the words already feel familiar.

## Before you start

- **An AI assistant with chat** (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat, DeepSeek or similar). A free account works; a paid plan may unlock smoother voice mode.
- **A device with a microphone** if you want to rehearse spoken — phone, tablet or laptop.
- **Your real numbers** in a notes app: your current pay, the figure you want, and one sentence about why you deserve it.
- **About 20–30 minutes** for a full rehearsal, or 5 minutes for one tricky moment.

## Step 1 — Pick your practice partner and open a fresh chat

Open the AI assistant you already use, then start a brand-new chat — look for a button like "New chat", "New conversation" or a small **+** icon. Starting fresh matters because the AI reads everything above; you don't want yesterday's dinner recipe muddying your salary rehearsal. After the chat opens, look for a way to talk to it — either a text box at the bottom of the screen, or a microphone icon 🎤 for voice mode.

If your app doesn't show a microphone icon, check a side menu or settings panel for something labeled "voice", "talk" or "speech". Some assistants keep voice mode on paid plans; if so, just type instead — it still works, just quieter.
💬 Example: *"I'd like to practice a salary conversation. Please play the role of my manager and stay in character the whole time."*

You'll know it worked when the AI replies *as* your manager (something like "Hi, you wanted to chat?") rather than giving you tips on how to negotiate.

## Step 2 — Set the scene with the real details

Before you start speaking, type a short briefing: your name, your role, your current pay, the figure you want, and one or two reasons. Think of it like giving the AI a script before a play — without these details it will improvise, and the practice will feel fake. After you send the briefing, the AI usually replies with a short acknowledgement or an opening question.

If the AI forgets the details halfway through, copy and paste the briefing again — most assistants lose track after a long chat, and a quick refresh puts them back on script.
💬 Example: *"I'm a marketing coordinator on $78,000. I'm asking for $88,000 because I've taken on the social media lead's work and my last review was 'exceeds expectations'. Please stay in character as my manager and don't break role to give me advice."*

You'll know it worked when the AI responds *as the manager*, using your actual numbers — not when it says "Great question! Here's how to negotiate".

## Step 3 — Practice the opening line out loud

Here's the bit everyone mumbles. So actually say it, even if you're alone in the kitchen. Use voice mode if you have it, or read your opening aloud while typing it. The aim isn't to sound slick — it's to feel the words in your mouth. Speak slowly, pause, then wait for the AI to answer in character. The first time will feel clunky; that's the whole point.

If voice mode cuts you off or mishears you, switch to typing the same words — hearing yourself *read* them out loud still counts.
💬 Example: *"Thanks for the time today. I'd like to talk about my salary. Based on the extra responsibilities I've picked up and my last review, I think $88,000 is the right number for me now."*

You'll know it worked when the words feel a little less scary the second time you say them — that's the point of this step.

## Step 4 — Run the awkward pushback moment

Every salary talk has a moment where the other person pushes back. "Tight budget." "Not this cycle." "Let's revisit in six months." Ask the AI to give you its strongest objection, then practice answering calmly. Don't dodge it — face it. The first answer will sound stiff; that's fine. Try it again with different words. This is where you find the phrasing that feels most like you, not the phrasing from a script.

If the AI is too nice and agrees too quickly, tell it: "Push back harder, like a real manager would." A good practice partner makes you work for the conversation.
💬 Example: *"Now push back hard. Tell me the budget is frozen until next financial year and there's nothing we can do."*

You'll know it worked when you can answer "I hear you, and I'd still like us to find a way" without apologising, rushing, or shrinking your voice.

## Step 5 — Practice the close

The end of a salary chat is where most people fold. Practice two endings: one where you hold your figure, and one where you accept a smaller offer but lock in a clear review date in writing. Say the words out loud, then say them again. The closer you can get to sounding matter-of-fact rather than pleading, the more weight your words carry in the room.

If the AI starts coaching you instead of staying in character, gently remind it: "Stay in role, please — you're still my manager." Coaching later; acting now.
💬 Example: *"I appreciate the offer of $83,000 with a review in six months. Can we put that review date and the goals in writing today, so we're both clear on what 'exceeds expectations' looks like?"*

You'll know it worked when you can say the closing sentence in one steady breath, looking at the screen like you mean it.

## Step 6 — Save your best lines and do one more pass

Scroll back through the chat and copy the two or three lines that sounded most like *you* — not the slickest, the most natural. Paste them into your notes app under "salary lines I actually like saying". Then start a fresh chat, give the same briefing, and try the opening again. The second run-through is usually the one that sticks, because you already know what to skip and what to slow down on.

If you don't have time for two full passes, at least do the opening twice. The first run finds the words; the second run makes them yours.
💬 Example: *"Round two. Same role, same numbers. Please start the conversation again from the top."*

You'll know it worked when you can say your opening line without reading it, and it sounds like something you'd actually say in a real meeting.

## Common mistakes

- **Just typing in your head and skipping the "out loud" part.** Reading your opening on a screen isn't rehearsal — your voice, breath and timing matter. Force yourself to speak.
- **Asking the AI for advice *during* the role-play.** It breaks character and ruins the practice. Get the rehearsal done first, then ask "How did I do?" at the end.
- **Practicing with fake numbers.** If you use $100,000 when you really want $88,000, you'll fumble when the real figure lands. Use the actual number, even if it feels scary.
- **Stopping after one pass.** The first run is messy on purpose. The second run is where the words stop feeling like lines and start feeling like yours.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** Any high-stakes conversation — asking for a refund, telling a landlord about a repair, setting a boundary with a relative — gets easier when you've said the words out loud first. An AI is a private, judgement-free place to rehearse.
- **For your work or business:** Negotiation isn't just salary. Pitching a project, asking for a deadline extension, pushing back on scope creep — same skill, same chat pattern works for all of them.
- **If you're just getting started:** Skip Steps 4 and 5 for now. Just rehearse the opening line from Step 3, twice. That's already most of the win.

## Try it now

Open your AI assistant right now, start a fresh chat, and send this single message: *"Please play my manager. I'm asking for a raise from $78,000 to $88,000 because I've taken on extra work and got a strong review. Stay in character the whole time, and start by saying 'Hi, you wanted to chat about your pay?'"* — then answer that one line out loud. Two minutes, one sentence, and you've already practiced more than most people ever do.
